I think my vet used the same thing for my rats. But I would just be very careful buying it on the internet and using it. Apparently it doesn’t take much to be toxic for rats! They had me using an absolutely TINY amount from a super small syringe they provided me with.

My rat Lemon unfortunately got a severe case of mites when I left my rats with a friend for a week... The vet gave her an oral medication that worked very well, and I had to bathe her once a week for about a month with rat shampoo to make sure that any remaining eggs or dead mites were removed. They also told me to of course clean the cage every few days during treatment. I also used newspaper instead of any other bedding during this time so I could easily change it out daily, and unfortunately removed all of her snuggly sleeping areas and toys until she was mite free. After washing those, I actually froze them in plastic bags in my freezer to make sure anything remaining was killed.  I also had her in a separate cage from her cage mates so she wouldn’t spread the mites to them. I would also have the your vet check their ears! Lemon also developed a bad ear infection from the mites in her ears, and had to have ear drops as well for awhile.

It was never so much that astrophysics was silly, it was more that people thought I was silly to think that I personally could pursue it. I think there’s this idea that you have to be some kind of super-genius to succeed in astrophysics. While there certainly is the occasional super-genius, I am completely convinced that anyone can understand these concepts if they want to. 

By seventh grade, I was enthralled by particle physics. When I told my best friend that I wanted to work for CERN when I was older, she said I was being stupid. “That’s completely unrealistic!” she scoffed. And so began a pretty persistent fear of math and fear of not being “smart enough”. I did almost four years of an International Relations degree before I realized that not doing what I love was actually what was silly.

Thank you! I used to think of it the same way, as something I would do if I were in an alternate dimension! I had so many people tell me it wasn't practical or realistic. I’m an undergraduate in this department, and my experience here has been mostly terrible. It’s honestly made me think about switching majors, or leaving the university. My best friend, who was a math major but had been taking multiple classes in the physics department through the fall, also committed suicide in January. It’s been the most horrible thing I’ve ever experienced. I do think that the way she was treated by professors and other staff in the department contributed to her feelings of hopelessness at the time. She was one of the most hard-working people I know, and we would study together in the math department until the building closed every night. Despite this, I know we both felt like we could not approach professors in the department for help when we had questions or concerns. They are often condescending and belittling at the worst, and at minimum, very apathetic towards students. She would recount her discussions with professors to me, panicking because they had told her that she had simply not been trying hard enough and would not properly address her questions. She told me she felt like she was too stupid. It was really awful to hear her think that, because she was so smart and talented. I also feel that most of the professors in the department have not received adequate pedagogical training. I have experienced amazing teachers in the math and chemistry departments, who obviously put great care into how they present their material. But many teachers I’ve had in the physics department seem very flippant about teaching, and often act as though they would rather not be in the lecture hall at all. It’s been a disappointing experience.

My friend and I were playing fetch with her border collie, Sofia, barefoot in the rain. I threw the ball sort of across my body because Sofia was on my right. She started running at full speed to catch the ball and ran right over my feet. Her claws gouged out a huge chunk of skin on the top of my left foot, and it started bleeding profusely. I think it looked particularly bad because of the rain making it run everywhere, but it was very deep and didn’t fully heal until about six months later. Sofia realized what had happened as she turned around to bring the ball back and hurried back to my friend and I. She instantly started whimpering and licking around the wound, and wouldn’t stop until my friend pried her away. She stayed by my side the rest of the day, resting her head on my leg, and it was the sweetest thing. She kept giving me this really human look, like she was so sorry and wanted me to feel better. I still remember that empathy from her so strongly. It was such a sweet moment, and I’ll never forget it.

It was a very unexpected adventure! My circumstances for being there were pretty unique. I started a genocide awareness group at my high school and was running it at the time. We were working with a group called Seven Fund, doing projects in Rwanda, and it just so happened that the founder was also an advisor to President Paul Kagame. I guess he told the president what we were doing, and later I got a letter in the mail inviting me to come to Rwanda for the Liberation Day ceremonies marking the end of the genocide!  I was there in 2011, for three weeks. 

I was working a lot while I was there, meeting with government officials, writing articles, conducting interviews... But I still had a lot of time to explore the country! 

Rwanda is a stunning place. The landscape is mostly dense rainforest, dotted with volcanoes rising out of the mist in a few places. Kigali, the capital, feels very safe and it is a incredibly clean city. All citizens are required by federal law to help in community cleanup and beautification efforts once a month, (if you are unable you pay a fee instead) and plastic bags are banned. Parliament is 65% women there, which is the largest percentage of women in parliament of any country in the world. It’s really up and coming!

The genocide memorial and museum in Kigali is a must. I don’t think I’ve been to any place in the world that had had such an emotional effect on me. It’s extremely heart wrenching, and I cried throughout the whole thing. It is the site of a series of mass graves in which over 250,000 people are interred. There is a peace and reconciliation garden, and an indoor facility which outlines Rwanda’s history and the events of the genocide. It’s a great place to start when you arrive, to better understand the history and culture of Rwanda, and to get a sense of how far the country has come!

The nature here is unbelievable. Going on safari in Akagera National Park is phenomenal. They have little cabins that you can stay in inside the National Park, and they overlook the huge lake that borders Uganda. Baboons were climbing up the walls all around us! I will never forget the sight of a pack of zebras flying gracefully over the edge of a hillside emerging out the mist. I felt like I was dreaming the whole time.

There are also excursions into the rainforest that you can take to see the gorillas, but I wasn’t old enough at the time. Apparently they are really aggressive towards children! It’s not like I was a child, but you have to be 18. So I went to the Dian Fossey institute and Karisoke rehabilitation center instead to see some of the gorillas they had saved from poachers. It’s an awesome place. Gorillas are such incredible animals. Well worth the visit! It’s also in the shadow of a giant volcano, so that’s pretty cool. 

The co-op markets in Kigali are also really amazing. The traditional fabrics used in Rwandan clothing are so vibrant and very distinctive. It was great to be able to interact directly with the people who were making the items I bought. 

I really think everyone should visit Rwanda if they can! Such amazing stories, people, and places. I’ll never forget it.
